title: Hundreds charged with assaulting or impeding immigration agents. Nearly half the cases that ended were lost or abandoned.
dek: The Times counted 558 people charged under 18 U.S.C. § 111, and 213 cases dismissed or acquitted. Three months on, Reuters and the AP have found the same pattern, judges have found agents’ accounts contradicted by video, and DHS says assaults are up 1,600 percent. The record, and what the government says.
body:
The New York Times counted them in July: 558 people charged since the start of 2025 with assaulting, resisting or impeding a federal officer, the crime at 18 U.S.C. § 111, in connection with the administration's immigration enforcement [1]. Of the cases that had ended, nearly half had been dismissed, lost at trial or quietly withdrawn: 191 dismissals and 22 acquittals, against 246 guilty pleas and four convictions by a jury, with 95 still pending [2]. In more than 100 of the cases the government alleged no injury to anyone; in at least seven, the injury an agent reported had been caused by the agents themselves or their colleagues [1].

Three months on, the picture the Times drew has not improved for the government. Reuters, counting every assault-on-officer case the department filed from January 2025 to March, found 31 percent of the completed ones dismissed, against a federal norm of about 8 percent; among the immigration-protest cases that had ended by May, about 45 percent had been dropped [3]. The Associated Press, in September, followed 102 felony arrests in Los Angeles, Chicago, Portland and Washington and found 41 percent dismissed outright and another 34 percent pleaded down to misdemeanors; a dozen had gone to trial on the felony charge, and not one had produced a conviction [4]. In the same months the Department of Homeland Security, under a new secretary, raised its own figure for assaults on its officers to an increase of more than 1,600 percent [5].

Both of those things can be true at once, and this report is an attempt to lay out how. It draws on the court records that the Times, Reuters, the AP, ProPublica and local newsrooms have assembled, on the Justice Department's own memos, and on what the department and the agency have said in their defense.

## The statute that does the work

Section 111 is an old law with a wide mouth. It punishes anyone who “forcibly assaults, resists, opposes, impedes, intimidates, or interferes with” a federal officer doing an official job [6]. It comes in three sizes. Simple assault is a misdemeanor, with a year as the maximum. Where the act involves physical contact or an intent to commit another felony, the maximum is eight years. Where a deadly weapon is used or someone is injured, it is twenty [6].

Two features make it unusually easy to charge and unusually hard to prove. The first is the list of six verbs, which lets an arrest for “impeding” be written up in the same breath as one for assault; the protester who stands in front of a vehicle and the one who throws a bottle at it are charged under the same section, and the complaints often read alike. The second is the word “forcibly,” which every court of appeals to consider the question reads as modifying all six verbs, so that following, filming and observing agents, without more, is not a crime under it [7]. The circuits disagree about how much more it takes. The Ninth Circuit, which covers Los Angeles and Portland, has held since 2008 that every conviction under the section requires some form of assault; the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth and Seventh, the last of which covers Chicago, hold that forcible resistance or impeding will do without one [8]. A petition asking the Supreme Court to resolve the split, which pointed out that the government keeps charging conduct short of assault wherever the question is open, was turned down in February without comment, so the line stays where each circuit has drawn it [8][9].

In practice the felony tier turns on physical contact, and physical contact is what the government has most often failed to show. The department's own resource manual, written long before this administration, tells prosecutors that force is an essential element, and that a threat counts as force when a reasonable officer would expect bodily harm from it [10].

## How the cases came apart

The pattern repeats across the districts where enforcement surged, with local variations.

**Washington.** After the federal takeover of the city's policing in August 2025, grand juries refused to indict at least seven times in five cases within a month [11], something former federal prosecutors described as exceptionally rare [12]. Sean Dunn, who threw a sandwich at a Border Patrol agent, was refused a felony indictment, recharged with a misdemeanor and acquitted by a jury on November 6 [13]. Sidney Reid, who had been filming an arrest outside the city jail, was refused three times before a jury acquitted her of a misdemeanor in October; the judge in her case had told prosecutors that either the agent had lied or someone had been careless with the facts [14]. A magistrate judge, Zia Faruqui, put a number on the office's record in an October opinion: it had moved to dismiss 20 of the 95 cases it opened by complaint in eight weeks, against fewer than 20 of more than 4,000 such cases in the preceding decade [15]. The U.S. attorney, Jeanine Pirro, called the grand juries' refusals the essence of a politicized jury and said the system was broken [12]. A year on, of the 27 Section 111 cases brought in the first wave of the surge, 18 had been dismissed or cut to misdemeanors, three had ended in felony pleas and one had gone to trial, Dunn's [16].

**Chicago.** During Operation Midway Blitz in the fall of 2025, grand juries refused prosecutors at least three times in two months, in a district where the court could recall one such refusal this century; Magistrate Judge Gabriel Fuentes wrote that the office had “swung and missed” repeatedly [17]. A list DHS was ordered to produce in a lawsuit over its tactics in the city showed 92 arrests for assaulting or impeding agents, of which 54 had not been charged, 20 had been declined by prosecutors, 13 had been charged and then dismissed and five were pending; none had produced a conviction [18]. The Times' later count for the district was 62 people charged, 59 cases dropped or dismissed, one guilty plea and no conviction at trial; Chicago alone accounted for more than a quarter of the failures nationwide [19]. The largest case, a conspiracy charge against six protesters arrested outside the Broadview facility, came apart in stages: two defendants were dropped in March, the felony conspiracy count in April, and on May 21 the U.S. attorney moved to dismiss the remaining misdemeanors with prejudice after Judge April Perry, having read the unredacted grand jury transcripts, described a prosecutor who had put her own credibility behind the charges, had communicated with grand jurors outside the room and had excused jurors who disagreed with the government; the trust she normally extended to the office, the judge said, had been broken [20]. In September a career prosecutor on the case retired under protest, saying the U.S. attorney had ordered the felony charge over her objection, which the department denies [21]; on October 1 Perry ordered sworn fact-finding into whether prosecutors had been candid with her [22].

**Los Angeles.** The first wave of felony cases after the June 2025 raids went badly from the start: of the first nine, seven were dismissed, and in several the agents' accounts were contradicted by video or, in one, by the agent's own admission that he had misstated the order of events [23]. The Los Angeles Times reported that July that career prosecutors had refused to sign some of the charging documents and that the U.S. attorney, Bill Essayli, had told a subordinate to disregard the Justice Manual's rule that a case should be brought only if it can be won at trial; his office called the account anonymous gossip [24]. One of the first to reach a jury, against a man whom the Border Patrol sector chief Gregory Bovino testified he had seen strike an agent, ended in an acquittal in about an hour after the video showed the agent shoving him [25]. By April the office had lost all five of the assault cases it had taken to trial [26]. In December, when a Los Angeles jury acquitted a tow-truck driver charged with theft for towing an ICE vehicle, the White House deputy chief of staff, Stephen Miller, called the verdict jury nullification in a blue city [27].

**Minnesota and the rest.** The enforcement surge of early 2026 in Minneapolis, in which agents shot and killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti, produced about three dozen Section 111 cases; of the 20 resolved by September, 19 had been dismissed [28], and all 16 of the defendants the attorney general had publicized in January had seen their felonies cut to misdemeanors [29]. Two men charged with assault after agents shot one of them on January 14 were un-charged a month later, after the acting ICE director acknowledged that two officers had given untruthful statements [30]; Hennepin County prosecutors later charged one of the agents [31]. The U.S. attorney, Daniel Rosen, said in June that none of his cases had failed in any way [31] and that bodily harm is not the measure of a serious crime [32]. In San Antonio, a federal judge dismissed a case in October 2025 after video showed that the officer had cut himself breaking a car window, calling the government's account largely fictional [33]; the dismissal was with prejudice, and the government has appealed [34]. In San Diego, ten of the 22 such cases filed in the administration's first year were dismissed, against two of 25 the year before [35].

What links these is the camera. The Times found two cases in which judges concluded that agents had destroyed evidence, including one in which an agent made a defendant delete the pictures on a phone, and more than two dozen in which the defendant was charged for filming or following agents with no physical contact alleged at all [2]. In case after case the reporters followed, bystander and body-camera footage, which did not exist in this volume a decade ago, told a different story from the arrest report.

## What the government says

The Justice Department does not dispute the counts so much as the conclusion. A spokesman, Wyn Hornbuckle, told the Times that prosecutors are right to prioritize these cases and that charges are sometimes reduced or dropped for mitigating factors; a department official said some were dropped because the defendant had already been deported [2]. The department told the AP that each case stands on its facts and that prosecutors are obliged to disclose mitigating evidence and sometimes downgrade charges because of it; the Los Angeles office said its prosecutions answered a wave of violence and that some charges were voluntarily dismissed after further investigation [4]. Two officials familiar with the instructions told Reuters something else as well, anonymously: that prosecutors had been required to explain any declination to Washington, which pushed weak cases forward [3].

The department's leaders intend to keep charging. Todd Blanche, as acting attorney general in May, told a border-security conference in Phoenix that the department would take every case in which someone touches an officer in an aggressive way and prosecute it [36]. The attorney general's September 2025 memo on political violence against ICE had already directed the U.S. attorneys in Oregon and northern Illinois to bring the highest provable charge in every such case [37], and a December memo implementing the president's directive on domestic terrorism told prosecutors to charge every federal crime they encountered to the fullest extent, listed Section 111 first among the statutes to keep in mind, and directed them to seek a terrorism enhancement where one applied [38].

The agency's case rests on the proposition that its officers face a wave of attacks, and some of the attacks are not in dispute. On July 4, 2025, a group set off fireworks and vandalized vehicles at the Prairieland detention center in Alvarado, Texas, and a police officer answering the call was shot in the neck; in June eight defendants were sentenced to terms from 30 to 100 years [39]. In September 2025 a gunman firing from a rooftop into the Dallas ICE field office killed one detainee and critically wounded two others, one of whom died days later, before killing himself; unspent rounds at the scene carried anti-ICE messages [40][41]. In June 2025 a Minnesota man drove off with an ICE officer's arm trapped inside his car and dragged him more than a hundred yards; a jury convicted the driver in December of assault with a dangerous weapon causing bodily injury [42], and the officer, Jonathan Ross, needed 33 stitches [43]. In Portland a protester who hit an officer in the head with a rock pleaded guilty and was sentenced in June to 30 months [44]. Earlier this month someone threw an incendiary device at an ICE building in Atlanta; it failed to clear the perimeter fence [45]. Those cases are real, and they are the ones the department points to.

## The numbers behind the percentages

What is in dispute is the arithmetic that turns them into a surge. DHS's figure has climbed as the year went on: 413 percent in June 2025, 690 percent on July 1, more than 1,000 percent by August, more than 1,150 percent in November, 1,347 percent in January and, from the new secretary, Markwayne Mullin, in September, 1,649 percent [46][47][48][49][5]. On the occasions the department has given the raw counts, they were small: 10 assaults in the first five months of 2024 against 79 in 2025; 19 in 2024 against 238 by November and 275 by the end of the year [47][48][49]. Mullin's figure compares 647 assaults in the first 20 months of this term with 37 in the same stretch of the Biden administration, a baseline the department had not used before [50].

The department has not released the list of incidents behind any of these figures or explained how they were counted [46], has declined to say how it defines an assault [51], and did not provide the list to Colorado Public Radio, the Los Angeles Times or the AP when they asked [46][52][51]. Reporters who went to the courts instead found a rise, but a far smaller one. Nationwide, federal assault-on-officer charges in 2025 ran about 25 percent above 2024 through mid-September, and most of the quarter-over-quarter jump was Los Angeles [46]. Across the five busiest districts, the Los Angeles Times counted 163 such cases from January through November 2025 against 129 the year before, an increase of 26 percent from a 2024 baseline that was itself inflated by the January 6 prosecutions; in just over half the 2025 cases the officer reported no physical injury, and 26 involved a serious one [52]. The Border Patrol's own count showed 174 assaults on its agents in the first half of 2025, slightly fewer than the 184 in the same months of 2024 [53]. Justice Department records analyzed by TRAC at Syracuse University show that the agency's referrals under the section did set a record in fiscal 2025, 274 cases, roughly double the pre-pandemic level, a real change and a much smaller one than a thousand percent [54].

Two explanations are offered for the gap, and they are not exclusive. One, from former ICE officials, is that the court record understates assaults because prosecutors decline the minor ones [46], and that daylight street arrests of the kind the agency now conducts produce more confrontations than the targeted arrests of the past [52]. The other is scale: the Cato Institute's David Bier points out that street arrests themselves are up nearly 500 percent [55], and a percentage built on a base of ten or nineteen says very little in any case. Charis Kubrin, a criminologist at the University of California, Irvine, called the framing a moral panic built on a near-zero baseline [52].

## The directives

The dismissals did not happen in a vacuum, and neither did the charging. The attorney general's first-day memo in February 2025 told prosecutors to charge the most serious readily provable offense and named the protection of law enforcement among the department's priorities [56]. By November the deputy attorney general's office was asking U.S. attorneys for examples of judicial obstacles met in cases involving assaults on officers, obstruction of immigration enforcement and Antifa, and an unnamed department spokesman described the judges in question as liberals in robes [57]. The Times reported in March that a senior aide to Blanche, Aakash Singh, had told prosecutors on a January conference call to go big and go loud with protest indictments; the Broadview defendants, now cleared, have asked the court for the communications between Blanche's office and the local prosecutors [58].

The courts have answered institutionally as well as case by case. The Northern District of Illinois put a rule into effect in May requiring that a grand jury's refusal to indict in a complaint case be docketed publicly, where before it left no public trace [59]. Federal grand juries declined to indict about 15 times a year in the decade through 2016, the last year for which the government published the figure, and six times in that final year, out of more than 150,000 matters [60][15]; Just Security counts at least 18 publicly reported refusals under this administration [15], and a defense-bar tracker counted 13 jury trials on these charges through March, ten of them acquittals [61]. In 2024, 82 percent of federal defendants charged with assault were convicted [4]. The department has answered in its own way: on September 30 it filed a judicial-misconduct complaint with the Eighth Circuit against two federal judges in Minnesota, Patrick Schiltz and John Tunheim, and against unnamed colleagues of theirs, over interviews in which the two criticized the enforcement surge in their district [62].

## What to watch

- **The felony line.** With the Supreme Court having declined in February to settle what “forcibly” requires, the same conduct can be a felony in Chicago and no crime at all in Los Angeles. The next petition that presents the question cleanly will matter [8][9].
- **Chicago's fact-finding.** Judge Perry's inquiry into the prosecutors' candor before her, and the defendants' request for the communications between Blanche's office and the local prosecutors, will show how much of the charging was directed from Washington [22][58].
- **The judges' complaint.** The complaint against Schiltz, Tunheim and their colleagues asks that they be kept off DHS matters. How the Eighth Circuit handles it will be read in every district that has criticized the department [62].
- **The other direction.** On Friday a Harris County grand jury indicted an ICE officer for aggravated assault after he struck a man with his vehicle during a pursuit in Houston; ICE called the indictment a political stunt. State prosecutions of federal officers raise questions of federal immunity that the protester cases do not [63].
- **A list.** DHS has shifted its comparison windows and, lately, its baseline. A list of the incidents, with dates and dispositions, would settle most of the argument above. None has been released [46][50].
